text:
A has a factual error: **"The job was stopped after 35 minutes."** The report never says when the job started. It only says the first call came at 8:20am, 14 calls had arrived by 9am, and the job was stopped at 9:35am. The "35 minutes" figure seems to count from 9:00, a point that has no meaning for the job. It is unsupported, and if measured from the first known report it is wrong (75 minutes). A busy manager would likely repeat this figure. A also omits two things the manager needs. First, the "we've been hacked" all-staff message leaked and was quoted in local news, which is a reputational issue. Second, there is a dated action (comms guide update, due 31 October) to stop it happening again. A is well within the 120-word limit (about 105 words) and otherwise accurate.

B is accurate on dates, numbers and status: change on 1 October, 347 statements, the data exposed, regulator notified on 3 October, members phoned by 6 October, a second reviewer from 13 October, the comms guide by 31 October, and remaining statements on 9 October. Its only slip is calling the all-staff "message" an "email," which is minor. It includes the media leak and the comms fix, both relevant to a manager. Its weakness is length: about 144 words, which breaks the "under 120 words" instruction. That is a real failure, but it does not mislead the reader.

Weighing them, the rubric puts accuracy first. A gives a manager a fabricated figure and leaves out the reputational issue. B is accurate and complete but too long. B is the better summary, with its length overrun as a clear deduction.

Verdict: B
